metaDescription: Five Breville food processors compared: Sous Chef 9, 12 and 16 cup plus the Paradice dicing models, with notes on size, storage and which suits you.
expertTake: The Sous Chef 16 is the best overall pick because the large bowl and full disc set cover nearly every prep job. The Sous Chef 9 is the value choice for small households that still want the brand's storage design. Skip the Paradice dicing models unless you actually dice onions, peppers and potatoes by the bagful.
introParagraphs: This Australian maker sits at the premium end of the home food processor market, and its machines share a family look: brushed steel finish, a heavy base and a storage caddy built into the unit. The range comes in three bowl sizes and two feature tiers.

Because the models are so similar in appearance, buyers often pick on looks and discover the capacity or the dicing system did not match their cooking. Sorting by bowl size first, then by whether you want a dedicated dicing kit, avoids that mistake.

products.name: Breville BFP810 Sous Chef 16-Cup Food Processor

specList.label: Cuts
specList.value: Slice, shred, French fry, mince, puree

products.description:
The Sous Chef 16 is the flagship of the standard line, a 16-cup machine built for precision and consistent size. A full set of discs covers slicing, shredding and French fry cutting, and the S-blade minces and purees, so one machine handles nearly every prep job a home cook has. The brand also ties the machine to an app with a library of guided recipes, a nice extra though not a performance feature.

What the 16-cup size buys you is room. A head of cabbage for coleslaw, several pounds of potatoes for latkes or a big batch of dough for a holiday weekend all fit without working in rounds. The heavy base and brushed steel body keep the machine planted when the disc is working through dense food, and the onboard storage keeps the sharp parts on the machine instead of loose in a drawer.

The cost of capacity is size and money. It is the tallest machine in the family, takes real counter space and sits at the top of the price ladder among the standard models. If you cook in volume, it earns its place. If you cook for one or two, the Sous Chef 9 does the same jobs in a smaller footprint, and you would rarely fill a 16-cup bowl.
products.bestFor: Large households and serious cooks who prep in volume and want every cut.
pros: Slice, shred, French fry, mince and puree
cons: Tall and wide on the counter

products.name: Breville BFP710 Sous Chef 12-Cup Food Processor
products.description:
The Sous Chef 12 is the middle child, and for many households it is the right size. Twelve cups handle a family salad, a double batch of dip and most weekend baking, yet the machine is shorter than the 16 and far easier to lift. The integrated storage caddy houses the S-blade and the reversible shredder along with the other discs, so the whole kit lives on the base.

Where it sits in the family matters. Compared with the 16-cup, it gives up volume and a few specialty cuts, and it costs less. Compared with the 9-cup, it gains three cups of room and loses some of the compact charm. The brand's recipe library is available as with the other models, and it is useful for a new owner learning what the discs do.

Ownership follows the family pattern. The discs are hand-wash items for sharpness, the bowl and lid go on the top rack, and the caddy needs a wipe to keep crumbs from lodging in its slots. The 12 is the model to choose if you want the brand's quality and storage without committing to a very large machine.
products.bestFor: Families who want brand quality and storage in a mid-size bowl.
pros: Twelve cups is right for most families
Storage caddy houses blade and discs

products.name: Breville BFP610 Sous Chef 9-Cup Food Processor
products.description:
The Sous Chef 9 is the compact member of the line, and its pitch is precision and performance in a smaller body. An onboard storage caddy keeps the blade and discs on the machine, the same system as the bigger models, so the benefit of tidy storage is not lost when you drop in size. By its listing it chops, slices, shreds and dices.

Nine cups is enough for a salad for four, a pound of cheese or a batch of hummus, which is the work most small households do. The smaller bowl also means the blade and discs sit closer to the food, and short chopping jobs come out more evenly than in a very large bowl. It is the one to choose for a flat, a small kitchen or someone who wants the steel look without the bulk.

In use it is the easiest to store and lift. Top-rack washing suits the bowl and lid; the discs are better done by hand, and the caddy should stay dry. It is not the machine for big holiday batches, so if you often cook for ten, step up to the 12 or the 16. For everyday cooking, it is the sensible entry to the brand.
products.bestFor: Small households and apartments that want the brand's storage and finish.
pros: Compact footprint for a premium machine
Onboard caddy stores blade and discs
cons: Premium price for a small bowl

products.name: Breville BFP838 Paradice 16 Food Processor and Dicer
products.description:
The Paradice 16 is the Sous Chef 16 with a dicing kit in the box. A dicing attachment slices and then cuts crosswise in one pass, turning onions, peppers, potatoes and celery into uniform cubes for soup bases, salsas and roasting trays. Uniform cubes cook evenly and look professional, which is why the brand pitches the machine for presentation.

If you dice a lot, the kit is a real time-saver. A pile of vegetables that would take twenty minutes with a knife goes through in a couple of minutes. If you rarely dice, the kit is an expensive extra, and you are paying for a feature you will leave in the drawer. It sits at the top of the price range in this guide for that reason.

Ownership follows the 16-cup family. A big bowl, a heavy base, hand-wash discs and a lot of parts to store. The dicing kit's grid is the part to clean carefully, since vegetable fibers lodge in the blades and need a brush. For a cook who dices daily, it is the best tool in the group, and for everyone else the standard Sous Chef 16 is the smarter buy.
products.bestFor: Cooks who dice onions, peppers and potatoes in volume.
pros: Slice, shred and dice in one machine
cons: Dicing grid is fiddly to clean
Wasted money if you rarely dice

products.name: Breville BFP638 Paradice 9 Food Processor and Dicer
products.description:
The Paradice 9 combines the compact bowl of the Sous Chef 9 with a dicing kit. It chops, slices, shreds and dices, and it keeps the tidy onboard storage that makes the family worth owning. For a small household that does real cooking from scratch, this is the neatest way to get dicing without a very large machine.

The model comes in a range of finishes beyond brushed steel, such as blue, olive and black, which matters if the machine lives on the counter. The color is the main difference between the listings, and the machine itself is the same, so pick the finish that suits your kitchen.

Because a dicing kit adds parts, storage and cleaning take more attention than on the plain 9-cup. Brush the dicing grid after each use, store the discs in the caddy and wipe the base. If you dice weekly, it earns its place. If you do not, the standard Sous Chef 9 is cheaper and does almost everything else the same.
products.bestFor: Small households that dice often and want a compact machine.
pros: Dicing kit in a compact body

buyingCriteria.explanation: The family comes in 9, 12 and 16 cups, and capacity decides how you will use the machine. The Sous Chef 9 and Paradice 9 suit households of one to four, the Sous Chef 12 suits most families, and the Sous Chef 16 and Paradice 16 are for volume. A very large bowl is a handicap for small chopping jobs. Pick the size that fits your regular batch, not your biggest holiday dinner.

The Paradice models add a dicing kit that slices and cuts crosswise in one pass. It gives uniform cubes for soup bases, salsas and roasting, and it is only worth the extra cost if you dice often. A cook who dices an onion once a week can do it by hand in a minute. A cook who dices several onions, peppers and potatoes daily will save real time.

All of these machines use an integrated storage caddy that keeps the blade and discs on the base. That design solves the problem of lost discs and sharp edges loose in a drawer. Check that the caddy fits your counter or cabinet height. Remember that a caddy is another surface to wipe, and crumbs lodge in its slots.

The Sous Chef 16 lists slice, shred, French fry, mince and puree, and the 9 and 12 list chop, slice, shred and dice or similar. More cuts means more discs to store and keep sharp. Look at the cuts you actually use and ignore the rest. A French fry disc is fun, but the reversible shredder and slicer cover most weeknight cooking.

Premium processors are heavy and tall. The 16-cup models take real space and may not fit under a cabinet with the lid in place. Measure from the counter to the underside of your cabinet before you buy. A machine that must be lifted from a high shelf is a machine you stop using.

A brushed stainless body resists fingerprints and ages well, and the colored Paradice 9 options add choice. All of the machines use plastic bowls that scratch over time, and discs need hand washing to stay sharp. These are long-term appliances that reward careful use. A machine used weekly for years is better value than a cheaper one replaced in three.

specDecoder.watchFor: The Paradice 9 and Paradice 16 include it, and the Sous Chef models do not.

specDecoder.watchFor: The Paradice 9 also comes in colors, so check which listing you are buying.

howWeEvaluated.title: Size fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We matched the 9, 12 and 16-cup bowls to household sizes and batch types. A machine that is too big for daily use lost points. The Sous Chef 12 scored as the most broadly useful.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cut range
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared the disc sets and the dicing kits across the five models. The Sous Chef 16's slice, shred, French fry, mince and puree range and the Paradice dicing kit were weighed against what a home cook needs. More cuts only counted if they are likely to be used.

howWeEvaluated.title: Storage and footprint
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at the onboard caddy design and the height and weight of each model. Compact machines earned credit for small kitchens. A caddy that keeps sharp parts on the machine earned safety credit.

howWeEvaluated.title: Build and finish
howWeEvaluated.description: We reviewed the steel finish, base weight and available colors. Heavy bases resist walking under dense loads. Finish mattered for machines that live on the counter.

howWeEvaluated.title: Owner feedback patterns
howWeEvaluated.description: We read owner feedback for repeating themes such as cracked bowls, dull discs and dicing grid cleaning. Those patterns shaped the cons. Individual comments were never treated as measurements.

cards.label: Sous Chef
cards.text: The Sous Chef 9, 12 and 16 offer the standard disc set with storage. They cover chopping, slicing and shredding for most households. They cost less than the Paradice versions.

cards.label: Paradice
cards.text: The Paradice 9 and 16 add a dicing kit that cuts uniform cubes. They suit cooks who dice often. You pay more and take on a fiddly grid to clean.

howToChoose.note: Choose Sous Chef for general cooking. Choose Paradice only if you dice weekly.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Enough bowl for a week of vegetables, a full disc set and a heavy base. Storage that keeps sharp parts on the machine helps you reach for it often.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Sous Chef 12 is the best balance of size and storage, and the Sous Chef 16 is the pick for large households. The Paradice models add dicing if that is your weekly task.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You cook from scratch several times a week and dice or shred in volume. The Sous Chef 16 and Paradice 16 pay back in time saved.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You prep a few times a week. The Sous Chef 9 and the Sous Chef 12 give the brand's quality at a lower tier.

maintenance.why: Oils and acids stain plastic. Use warm soapy water or the top rack.
Dishwashers dull cutting edges. A brush keeps fingers clear of the sharp edge.
Vegetable fibers lodge in the grid and harden. Brush from the back so debris falls out.
Crumbs and moisture collect in the slots. Dry thoroughly before storing the discs.

maintenance.task: Inspect the lid and locking tabs
maintenance.why: A cracked tab can defeat the interlock. Replace the part rather than forcing it.

faq.a: For one or two people choose the 9-cup, for most families the 12-cup and for large households or heavy batch cooking the 16-cup. Bigger is not better for small jobs. Match the bowl to your regular batch.

faq.q: Is the Paradice worth the extra cost?
faq.a: Only if you dice vegetables often. The dicing kit gives uniform cubes in one pass and saves real time. If you dice rarely, the standard Sous Chef is the smarter buy.

faq.q: Are the different colors the same machine?
faq.a: For the Paradice 9, yes. The finish is the main difference between the listings. Check the box contents and warranty for the exact listing you buy.
Small batches of soft dough work, but check the manual for the load limit. Heavy bread dough in volume is better suited to a stand mixer. Do not overload the bowl.

faq.q: Do the guided recipes affect performance?
faq.a: No. The recipe library is an extra that helps you learn. The motor, bowl and discs determine performance.

faq.q: How long will one of these last?
faq.a: The motor base is built to last many years with sensible use. Bowls, lids and blades are the parts that wear. Hand washing the discs keeps them sharp for longer.
